RagShortTexts: After Alamut fell, Syrian assassins at Masyaf used hidden blades to survive among Mamluks.

Variants.Content: After Hulagu's Mongols destroyed Alamut in 1256, the Nizari Ismailis of Syria kept their communities alive through strongholds at Masyaf and Jabal Bahra. Lacking an army to match Mamluk or crusader forces, they relied on a silent network of informers and fida'i operatives who spent years living as servants, grooms, or merchants before a single strike. Since a murder could decide a succession, neighboring rulers often paid tribute to avert it. The community's survival depended on reputation: a lord who paid the tribute was left alone, while one who refused could expect a killing in his own pavilion.

No commander sleeps without trusted bodyguards posted at his door. Conrad of Montferrat was killed in Tyre in 1192 by men disguised as friars, which turned every lord's sleep into a question of who was in the next room. A late tribute payment to Masyaf brings anxious letters, and anxiety can cost a lord his household.

Never cross quiet travelers sitting alone in wayside inns. A slender dagger tipped with viper venom can slip between coat plates before a man can draw his arming sword. Guards on caravan routes check every stranger's hands, and a man who keeps his hood up and his belt loose is often questioned first. Soldiers who escort merchants learn to watch the crowd, not the road.
